name: Roberta Martin
description: Roberta Martin was a Chicago gospel singer, pianist, and songwriter who led the Roberta Martin Singers and stands, in CTL's gospel research, as the ensemble-and-training pipeline of Chicago gospel in one career. She worked as pianist at Ebenezer Baptist Church alongside Thomas A. Dorsey and Theodore Frye — a provenance documented in the Smithsonian's archival finding aid for the Roberta Martin collection. CTL's gospel brief places her inside the networked system — Dorsey's composing, Frye's chorus direction, Ebenezer's institutional base — that carried Chicago gospel from storefront and Holiness churches into mainline congregations and national circulation in the 1930s and 1940s. The graph record's era for her work is the 1940s–1960s, and her sources include the Gospel Music Hall of Fame.

name: Richard Hunt
description: Richard Howard Hunt was an American sculptor born September 12, 1935, on Chicago's South Side. He began youth classes at the Art Institute of Chicago at thirteen and received his B.A.E. from the School of the Art Institute of Chicago in 1957, developing the direct-welding technique in salvaged and new metal for which he became known. His Hero Construction (1958) entered the Art Institute's collection within a year of his graduation. In 1971 he became the first African American sculptor to receive a retrospective at the Museum of Modern Art in New York. Working largely in abstract welded metal on themes of flight, uplift, and emancipation, he completed more large-scale public commissions than any other American sculptor; his Chicago works include Jacob's Ladder (1977) at the Carter G. Woodson Library, Flight Forms (2002) at Midway Airport, and The Light of Truth Ida B. Wells National Monument (2021) in Bronzeville, and his Swing Low (2016) hangs in the Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History and Culture. He served on the governing board of the National Endowment for the Arts. Hunt died December 16, 2023, in Chicago, aged 88.

description: Romare Bearden was an American artist celebrated for paintings and collages drawn from African American life in the South, Pittsburgh, and Harlem. Born in Charlotte, North Carolina, he grew up mainly in Harlem, where his family's apartment drew writers, artists, and jazz musicians of the Harlem Renaissance. He graduated from New York University in 1935, studied at the Art Students League under George Grosz, and worked for much of his life as a New York City social-services caseworker while making art. After Army service and study in Paris on the G.I. Bill, he returned to New York. In 1963 he helped form Spiral, a collective of Black artists considering art's role in the civil rights movement, and his 1964 Projections exhibition of photomontage-based works brought him wide recognition; by 1966 he could support himself as an artist. Jazz and blues rhythms shaped his collage practice, and he also wrote on art. He received the National Medal of Arts a year before his death in New York in 1988.

description: University of Chicago sociologist (taught 1913–1933) whose 1937 supervisory trip to Bahia linked the Chicago school of sociology to Afro-Brazilian race-relations research.

name: Rotary Connection

name: Rose Records
description: Rose Records was a Chicago record-store chain whose locations stocked the dance-music imports and local pressings feeding the house era. The chain represents the mainstream-retail tier of the record-store ecology, alongside specialist shops like Importes Etc.

description: Chicago entrepreneur; founder of Dance Mania Records (1986-1999), the cornerstone Chicago house/ghetto house label; took over his family's Barney's One Stop Records distribution business in the mid-1980s; later ran New Life, the only health food store in North Lawndale.

name: Rev. 'Little' Lucy Smith
aliases: Little Lucy; Little Lucy Smith; Lucy Smith Collier
description: Lucy Smith Collier (1925-2010), 'Little Lucy': gospel singer, pianist, organist, and composer; Roberta Martin's stepdaughter and protege; vocalist, accompanist, and later pianist/musical director of the Roberta Martin Singers.

name: Ricky Dillard
description: Gospel singer Ricky Dillard sang on Farley 'Jackmaster' Funk's 1986 single 'Give Yourself to Me' (with Kevin 'Jack N House' Irving).

name: Robert Ford (writer/DJ)
description: Robert Ford was a Chicago DJ, designer, and writer who founded the THING zine in 1989, documenting Black queer house and ball culture. Ford's work bridges the journalist and dance-community nodes: a participant-documenter of the scene he wrote about.

name: Roland TR-808 Rhythm Composer
description: The Roland TR-808 drum machine (released 1980) was a foundational instrument of Chicago house — documented in the equipment history of Jesse Saunders' 'On & On' (1983–84). Chicago producers adopted the 808's deep bass drum as the rhythmic signature of house, a use-pattern distinct from its original design as a practice accompaniment.

name: Roland TB-303 Bass Line
description: The Roland TB-303 (released 1981, designed as a bass-guitar accompaniment) was repurposed by Chicago producers — documented on 'On & On' — and became the defining sound of acid house via Phuture's 'Acid Tracks.'. Ron Hardy's Muzic Box sets broke acid house to Chicago dancers, making the club — not the studio — the technology's proving ground.

name: Reel-to-reel and cassette mix-tape circulation
description: Reel-to-reel and cassette tape circulation was the distribution system that carried Chicago house music beyond the clubs before commercial distribution existed. Chicago's radio mix shows began on WGCI; rival WBMX answered by gathering street DJs as the Hot Mix Five, led by Kenny Jason and including Farley Keith Williams, later Farley Jackmaster Funk. Their thirty-minute mixes aired through the day — about eighteen records mixed as one continuous medley — and Saturday-night shows ran five hours, drawing between 250,000 and a million Chicago listeners. The Hot Mix Five's mixes were recorded on cassette tapes and sent across America and abroad. In the clubs, Ron Hardy worked from 1974 at Den One with turntables, a mixer, and a reel-to-reel deck, playing reel-to-reel edits, and Chicago producers debuted compositions at the Muzic Box through the acetates and tapes Hardy played. His reel-to-reel work circulated again in 2004–2005, in bootleg and authorized twelve-inch records of 'Ron's edits.'

name: Radio mix-show format (Hot Mix 5 model)
description: The radio mix-show format, in its Hot Mix 5 model, is the broadcast form WBMX built around live DJ blends on 'Saturday Night Live Ain't No Jive.' The Hot Mix 5 were a Chicago DJ team assembled by WBMX program director Lee Michaels in 1981: Farley 'Funkin' Keith, Mickey 'Mixin' Oliver, Ralphi Rosario, Kenny 'Jammin' Jason, and Scott 'Smokin' Silz. Their mixes turned the mix show into a broadcast technology for breaking records: the show rose to number one in Chicago ratings, took WBMX from worst to number one in the market, and broke house and Italo disco records for a mass audience beyond the clubs. CTL's research frames the format as a feedback loop in which producers could test records on air before pressing, collapsing the distance between club play and broadcast.

name: Roller-rink dance community
description: Chicago's Black roller rinks were dance floors in their own right -- skating venues where R&B, soul, and early house played and where skate-dance styles developed. Anchor venue The Rink was founded in 1975 by Carmen Clark and Nate Simpson at 8920 S Ashland Ave, moving in 1983 to 1122 E 87th St, where it remains. Spinning R&B 45s with a DJ (rather than a Wurlitzer organist) inspired "JB skating," a style rooted in James Brown's dancing -- crisscross footwork, dips, spins -- born on the South Side and since spread nationally. The rink circuit connected the disco-to-house transition for skaters who never entered the clubs, extending the dance floor's geography.

name: Reach Media
description: Texas-based media company founded by Tom Joyner with David Kantor in 2003 to own and distribute the Tom Joyner Morning Show; majority-owned by Urban One (Radio One) since 2004.

name: Readex African American Newspapers, 1827-1998
description: Commercial full-text archive of 350+ African American newspapers (1827-1998) in two series; the subscription-based counterpart to Chronicling America's free access.

name: Richelieu Dennis
description: Liberian-born founder of SheaMoisture/Sundial Brands (sold to Unilever 2017); creator of Essence Ventures, which acquired Essence in 2018; co-founder of Group Black; founder of the New Voices Fund.

name: Rescued Illinois Black Funeral-Home Burial Records
description: 140,000+ burial records from shuttered Black-owned funeral homes (dating to the 1880s), rescued by the Illinois Office of Comptroller and the Bronzeville Historical Society and transferred to CPL's Vivian G. Harsh Research Collection.

name: Rebuild Foundation (Stony Island Arts Bank)
description: Theaster Gates's Chicago nonprofit (founded 2010) revitalizing underinvested South Side neighborhoods through culture-based, artist-led projects; steward of the Stony Island Arts Bank.

name: Roberts Temple named to National Trust 11 Most Endangered
description: (2020) Roberts Temple Church of God in Christ (4021 S. State St., Bronzeville) named to the National Trust's 2020 list of America's 11 Most Endangered Historic Places; site of Emmett Till's 1955 open-casket funeral.

name: Royal Gardens / Lincoln Gardens
description: 31st Street jazz venue with documented Black ownership interests (1918-1921): Louis B. Anderson, William Bottoms, Virgil Williams (1918); Florence Majors (1921). King Oliver's Creole Jazz Band played there 1923-24.

name: Rosenwald Courts (Michigan Boulevard Garden Apartments)
description: 1929 Rosenwald-funded apartments; closed 2000; saved through a ~two-decade resident campaign and rebuilt as $132M mixed-use affordable housing in 2016.

name: Rev. Junius C. Austin / Rev. D.Z. Jackson / Rev. A.P. Jackson
aliases: Rev. Junius Caesar Austin Sr.; Rev. D.Z. Jackson (Durmon Z. Jackson); Rev. A.P. Jackson (Abraham Patterson Jackson)
description: Three Chicago Baptist pastors (group record): Rev. Junius Caesar Austin Sr., pastor of Pilgrim Baptist Church (Jan 1926-Aug 1968), who hired Thomas A. Dorsey in 1932; Rev. D.Z. Jackson (Durmon Z. Jackson), minister of Liberty Baptist Church from 1925, growing it to 3,000+ members; Rev. A.P. Jackson (Abraham Patterson Jackson, 1918-1994), son of D.Z. Jackson, pastor of Liberty Baptist from April 12, 1951, for 43 years.

name: Robert Hall (clothing) / later Taste disco
aliases: Robert Hall Clothes (Englewood); Taste Disco Lounge; Taste
description: Former Robert Hall Clothes store at 6331 S. Lowe in Englewood (1950s-60s); the building later became the Taste Disco Lounge.

name: Regal Men's Shop
description: Men's clothing retail shop documented in a 1955 photograph at 63rd & Maryland in Woodlawn; a present-day directory lists 'Regal Mens Fashion' at 326 E. 47th St. (same-business identity unresolved).

name: Rothschild Liquors
description: Chicago liquor-store business with a long-standing 63rd Street (Woodlawn) location at 425 E. 63rd Street; additional South and West Side locations documented (Pershing Road, Cicero Avenue); the 63rd Street store is permanently closed.

name: Racine CTA station (Green Line, closed)
description: Opened February 25, 1907; closed January 9, 1994; did not reopen with the Green Line in 1996; stationhouse and canopy survive. Architect Earl Nielson; Greek Revival design (Preservation Chicago records it as Classical Revival — see CTL-CFL-002485). R.A.G.E. campaigns for reopening; $2M federal feasibility study funded.

name: Rayvon Fouché
description: Rayvon Fouche is a Northwestern University professor of Communication Studies and Journalism whose research examines cultural representation, racial identification, and technoscientific design, including how AI impacts the Black community.

description: Ethiopian computer scientist; first Black woman to earn a CS PhD at Cornell and first Black woman professor in UC Berkeley EECS; co-founded Black in AI and Mechanism Design for Social Good (MD4SG).

name: Robert Crawford
description: Seventeen-year-old Chicago student at Wendell Phillips High School who built a fully functioning wireless station -- homemade transmitter, receiver, and telegraph key -- with his own hands. Profiled by the Chicago Defender on January 8, 1916; identified that year as the only Black member of the local Wireless Club. Communicated by wireless with Key West, Florida, and Atlantic coast towns. One of the earliest documented Black amateur-radio operators in Chicago, active before commercial radio emerged after 1920.

description: American engineer and designer of electronic musical instruments. Designed the LM-1 (1980, first programmable drum machine with acoustic samples), the LinnDrum (1982), and co-developed the Akai MPC60 (1988); inventor of the tools, NOT of their hip-hop transformation. description: Independent safety-net hospital opened 1924 at 45 W. 111th Street, Chicago; serves the Far South Side's predominantly Black neighborhoods; labor-and-delivery services suspended October 2026 amid financial pressure; received a $4M Illinois Treasurer loan in 2017.

description: Pay-at-the-door house parties held to raise rent money: hosts charged admission (reportedly about 25 cents a head in Bronzeville), served food and drink, and hired or hosted musicians. Neighbors helped carry furniture back upstairs afterward.

name: Riding the CTA as Black Chicagoans - el trains, skip-stops, and transit boundaries
description: Everyday use of Chicago's el and buses by Black residents: the Green Line and Red Line serving Bronzeville; A/B skip-stop patterns experienced as racially coded; transit as a boundary system.

name: Record collecting as community archiving (Chicago soul 45s)
description: The practice of hunting, preserving, and documenting obscure Chicago soul 45s and LPs - collecting as historical rescue of neighborhood music.

name: Reading Ebony and Jet in the home
description: Keeping Ebony and Jet magazines on coffee tables, in waiting rooms, barbershops, and beauty salons - the household information ritual of Black America.

name: Rotating credit associations (susu / partner systems) — Chicago status unresolved
description: Informal rotating savings and credit associations (ROSCAs) -- susu/sou-sou (West Africa), Partner (Caribbean), sol, njangi, box-hand -- in which members contribute fixed sums at regular intervals and each period one member receives the pooled "hand." Interest-free, trust-based systems that served as seed capital for Black homes and businesses across the diaspora, notably through women-led savings clubs. Well documented across the Black diaspora, but no Chicago-specific documentation was located; marked Unresolved pending oral-history or archival research.

name: Rev. Dr. Willie T. Barrow
aliases: Willie Beatrice Taplin; "Little Warrior"; "High Priestess of Protest"
description: Chicago civil rights activist and minister (1924-2015): SCLC field organizer for MLK Jr. (1953-1965, incl. Selma); founding member of Operation Breadbasket; co-founder of Operation PUSH (1971); first woman executive director/CEO of a civil rights organization (1984); co-chair of the Rainbow/PUSH Coalition; associate minister of Vernon Park Church of God.

name: Rev. William Lambert
description: Pastor of Greater Mount Hope Baptist Church; 1962 Chicago delegate to Albany, Georgia; leader of the Clergy Alliance selective-buying campaign.

name: Rev. David J. Black
description: Pastor listed for First Presbyterian Church of Chicago (Wikipedia infobox; not independently corroborated).

name: Rapp and Rapp
description: Rapp and Rapp was the Chicago architectural firm of brothers Cornelius W. Rapp and George L. Rapp, designers of three documented South Side movie palaces in CultureTechLens's place research. Their Tivoli Theatre at 63rd and Cottage Grove — the first of Balaban & Katz's 'big three' — opened February 16, 1921: a French Baroque palace of 3,520 seats built for $2,000,000, with a two-story lobby and a 55-piece orchestra at its gala opening. Their Trianon Ballroom at 6201 South Cottage Grove, owned by Andrew and William Karzas and marketed as 'The World's Most Beautiful Ballroom,' opened December 6, 1922. Their Southtown Theatre at 610 West 63rd Street opened December 25, 1931, closed in August 1958, and was demolished in 1991.

name: Richard Allen
description: Founder of Mother Bethel AME Church and of the African Methodist Episcopal Church denomination; first bishop of the AME Church; co-founder of the Free African Society.

name: Rutgers University

description: City in Logan County, Kentucky; birthplace of Alice Dunnigan (1906).

name: Roc Nation
description: Entertainment company and record label founded by Jay-Z. Vic Mensa signed with Roc Nation in 2015.

name: Ronnie Sloan
description: Founder (1985) and president of the House-O-Matics dance crew; he booked DJs including DJ Deeon and DJ Slugo for the crew's parties at 51st, the Elks, and the projects, and gave DJ Rashad, DJ Spinn, and RP Boo their first shots on the turntables.

name: Robert Williams
description: Chicago house-music promoter and co-owner of the Warehouse nightclub; with Siegfried Schuh he relocated the club to 206 S. Jefferson in 1977 as 'Chicago's response to New York City's vibrant dance club scene,' and persuaded Frankie Knuckles to move from New York to become resident DJ.

name: Respectability politics debates in Black Chicago
description: The long-running Black Chicago debate — in churches, women's clubs, and the press — over whether 'respectable' behavior and self-presentation could advance racial uplift, a strategy historian Evelyn Brooks Higginbotham named the 'politics of respectability.'

name: Rainbow Coalition (Chicago, 1969)
description: Multiracial, anti-racist, working-class coalition formed in Chicago on April 4, 1969, uniting the largely Puerto Rican Young Lords of Lincoln Park, the Illinois Black Panther Party of the South and West Sides, and the Young Patriots of Uptown. Co-led by José "Cha Cha" Jiménez, Fred Hampton, and William "Preacherman" Fesperman; cooperated on survival programs and solidarity actions against poverty, displacement, and police brutality.

name: Rainbow Coalition formed (Chicago, 1969)
description: The original Rainbow Coalition is formed in Chicago in 1969, co-led by the Young Lords Organization and the Illinois Chapter of the Black Panther Party with the Young Patriots — a multiracial working-class alliance around housing, poverty, police brutality, and racial and economic inequality.

name: Richard Pegue
description: Chicago Black radio DJ (1960s–2000s); music director at WVON from 1968; fill-in DJ on FM WGCI in the late 1970s; his 1980s–1990s off-the-radio aircheck tapes preserve Chicago Black radio broadcasts.

name: Rhonesha Byng
description: CEO and founder of Her Agenda; co-founder (June 2020) of the Black Owned Media Equity and Sustainability Institute (BOMESI) with DéVon Christopher Johnson. With Johnson she built BOMESI into a network of 300+ Black-owned publishers reaching 90M+ households monthly, holding brands' 2020 diversity-ad-spend commitments accountable.

name: Renata Cherlise
description: Renata Cherlise is the Atlanta-based creative director, multidisciplinary visual artist, and founder/curator of the Black Archives multimedia platform (launched on Tumblr 2011; Instagram expansion 2015). Author of 'Black Archives: A Photographic Celebration of Black Life' (Ten Speed Press, 2023).

name: Radio One
description: Media company founded by Cathy Hughes in 1980 with the purchase of WOL-AM; the radio arm of Urban One.

name: Ruth Wells
description: North Lawndale homeowner whose testimony at the January 1968 community meeting of contract buyers galvanized the formation of the Contract Buyers League; a leader of the organization.

name: Richard Drew
description: Director of the Englewood Business Men's Association; spearheaded the Englewood Shopping Center's community integration (events, parades, concerts, radio broadcasts). Died in 1978, after which the association lost its community focus.

name: Raymond O'Neil
description: White theatre director who founded the Ethiopian Art Theatre (1922/1923); staged a jazz-band-accompanied Comedy of Errors and a Salome revised with African American features for the all-Black company.

name: Ramsey Lewis Trio at Harry's Show Lounge (June 1956)

name: Russell Lee
description: Russell Lee (1903–1986) was an American documentary photographer, born in Ottawa, Illinois, who became the most prolific photographer of the Farm Security Administration. Trained as a chemical engineer at Lehigh University, he left chemistry for painting and then photography, and in the fall of 1936 joined Roy Stryker's federal photography project. Living out of his car, he photographed in 29 states between 1936 and 1942 and produced some 19,000 of the roughly 63,000 prints in the Library of Congress's FSA collection — more than twice the output of any other photographer on the team, on which he was the longest-tenured member. He was known for technical innovation, including direct-flash photography indoors, and for sustained photographic essays on single communities. In 1941 he turned that method on Chicago's South Side, producing the apartment-house interiors, church processionals, tavern scenes, and 47th Street shoeshine stands that now anchor CultureTechLens's Cited Photo Archive.

name: Rube Foster
description: Andrew “Rube” Foster (born September 17, 1879, in Calvert, Texas; died December 9, 1930, in Kankakee, Illinois) was an American baseball pitcher, manager, and owner known as the father of Black baseball. A star pitcher for the Cuban X-Giants and the Philadelphia Giants, he earned his nickname in 1904 by outdueling major-league ace Rube Waddell in an exhibition game. As player-manager of the Leland Giants and then owner-manager of the Chicago American Giants, he built the era's preeminent Black professional team. On February 13, 1920, at the Paseo YMCA in Kansas City, Missouri, he founded the Negro National League — the first successful professional league for Black ballplayers — and served as its president. His health collapsed in 1926, and he died four years later. He was elected to the National Baseball Hall of Fame in 1981.

name: Roy Ayers
description: Roy Ayers (born Roy Edward Ayers Jr., September 10, 1940, in Los Angeles, California; died March 4, 2025, in New York City) was an American vibraphonist, composer, and producer. By family account, the five-year-old Ayers received his first vibraphone mallets from Lionel Hampton at a concert. After post-bop work in the 1960s, including recordings with flutist Herbie Mann and solo albums for Atlantic Records, he formed Roy Ayers Ubiquity — named for his 1970 album Ubiquity — and, on Polydor Records, helped pioneer jazz-funk, scoring the film Coffy (1973) and making Everybody Loves the Sunshine (1976), his best-known album. His catalog became one of the most sampled in popular music, and his influence on the generation that followed earned him the attributed honorific “Godfather of Neo Soul”; singer Erykah Badu called him “the king of neo-soul.” He recorded and performed across six decades.

name: Richard Long
description: Richard Long (1933-1986) was the preeminent American sound designer of the disco era, founder of Richard Long and Associates, known for bass-forward club systems that dancers felt physically as much as heard. The City of Chicago's landmark report credits Long with the Warehouse's custom sound system and places him as designer at Paradise Garage and Studio 54; secondary accounts credit him with more than 300 installations and Billboard's 1980 Best Disco Sound Design award. At the Warehouse his system is documented as intense, very loud, and palpable from the street, and Knuckles studied it with Long to master precise control of the room.

name: Rosa Parks
aliases: Rosa Louise McCauley; Rosa Louise McCauley Parks
description: Rosa Parks, born Rosa Louise McCauley on February 4, 1913, in Tuskegee, Alabama, was a civil rights activist whose refusal to surrender her seat on a segregated Montgomery bus became the catalyst of the modern civil rights movement. A seamstress at a Montgomery department store, she was no accidental actor: she had served as secretary of the Montgomery chapter of the NAACP from 1943 and worked in voter registration for years before her arrest. On December 1, 1955, she refused a driver's order to give her seat to a white passenger and was arrested and convicted under the city's segregation ordinances. Her arrest sparked the Montgomery bus boycott, begun December 5, 1955, under the Montgomery Improvement Association, which elected the young pastor Martin Luther King Jr. its president; the boycott lasted 381 days and ended in victory after the Supreme Court upheld a ruling that bus segregation was unconstitutional. Parks later moved to Detroit, worked on the staff of Representative John Conyers from 1965 to 1988, and co-founded the Rosa and Raymond Parks Institute for Self Development in 1987. She died in Detroit on October 24, 2005, aged 92.

name: Ruby Bridges
aliases: Ruby Nell Bridges; Ruby Bridges Hall; Ruby Nell Bridges Hall
description: Ruby Bridges is an American civil rights activist who, as a six-year-old first grader, became a defining figure of school desegregation in the American South. Born on September 8, 1954, in Tylertown, Mississippi, she moved with her family to New Orleans, Louisiana, at age four. On November 14, 1960, escorted by four federal marshals, she became the only Black student to enroll at the previously all-white William Frantz Elementary School, the youngest of a small group of African American children assigned to integrate New Orleans schools by court order. White parents withdrew their children, and for a full school year she was taught alone by Barbara Henry, the one teacher willing to teach her, attending every day despite daily protests and threats. She later worked as a travel agent, raised four children, and in 1999 founded the Ruby Bridges Foundation to promote tolerance, respect, and appreciation of difference through education. She received the Presidential Citizens Medal in 2001 and continues to speak and write for young readers about courage and equality.

name: Raphael Warnock
description: Raphael Gamaliel Warnock (born July 23, 1969, in Savannah, Georgia) is the United States senator from Georgia and, since 2005, the senior pastor of Ebenezer Baptist Church in Atlanta — the pulpit once held by Martin Luther King Jr. and his father. A Morehouse College graduate who earned his doctorate at Union Theological Seminary, Warnock pastored in Baltimore before Ebenezer called him as its fifth senior pastor. He entered the Senate by winning Georgia's January 5, 2021, runoff against Senator Kelly Loeffler, taking office on January 20, 2021, as the first Black senator in Georgia history and the first Black Democrat elected to the Senate from a Southern state. In 2022 he led Herschel Walker in the November general election, 49.4 percent to 48.5, and won the December 6, 2022, runoff for a full term. Warnock holds his two callings in one biography — the King pulpit and the King-era seat Georgia had never before given a Black citizen. With Scott, Booker, Blunt Rochester, and Alsobrooks, he completes the five — the most Black senators ever to serve simultaneously.

name: Reconstruction (1865–1877)
description: Reconstruction, the era the intake timeline names 'The Post-Slavery South,' ran from the end of the Civil War in 1865 to the Compromise of 1877, which withdrew the last federal troops from the South. In those twelve years the United States attempted — and then abandoned — the rebuilding of the former Confederacy on terms of racial equality. The Thirteenth, Fourteenth, and Fifteenth Amendments rewrote the Constitution: abolishing slavery, establishing birthright citizenship and equal protection, and prohibiting racial discrimination in voting. Under the Reconstruction Acts of 1867, Black men voted across the South, and more than 2,000 Black officeholders served at every level of government, among them Hiram Revels and Blanche K. Bruce in the United States Senate and P. B. S. Pinchback, who became governor of Louisiana (held at CTL-E-1524). Freedpeople built schools, churches, and families' legal foundations at extraordinary speed. The counterrevolution was equally systematic — paramilitary violence, Black Codes' successors, and finally redemption governments ended the experiment, and its constitutional amendments slept for nearly a century before the movement chronicled later in this timeline woke them.

name: Regents of the University of California v. Bakke decided (1978)
aliases: The Bakke Decision; Bakke Decision and Affirmative Action; Bakke v. Regents
description: On June 28, 1978, the United States Supreme Court decided Regents of the University of California v. Bakke, 438 U.S. 265, the case the intake timeline files as 'The Bakke Decision and Affirmative Action.' Allan Bakke, a white applicant twice rejected by the medical school at the University of California, Davis, had challenged the school's admissions program, which reserved sixteen of one hundred seats for minority students. A fractured Court produced no single majority opinion: four justices would have upheld the program, four would have ended all racial consideration under Title VI, and Justice Lewis Powell's lone opinion controlled the outcome — the Davis set-aside was unconstitutional and Bakke was admitted, but race could remain one factor among many in a holistic admissions process aimed at a diverse student body. Powell's diversity rationale governed university affirmative action for forty-five years, through Grutter in 2003, until the Court ended the practice in the Harvard and North Carolina cases of 2023. The graph's nearest prior record — Chicago's MWBE set-aside program (CTL-E-1354) — is affirmative action's municipal cousin, labeled NEAR in the audit; this record is the decision itself.

name: Roc (TV series)
description: Roc, created by Stan Daniels and produced by HBO Independent Productions, aired on Fox from August 25, 1991, to May 10, 1994 — three seasons, seventy-two episodes starring Charles S. Dutton as Roc Emerson, a Baltimore sanitation worker whose household absorbed his brother, his father, and the economics of a working-class Black family rendered without sentimentality. Its place in television history is a production feat: the series' entire second season was broadcast live, making it the first prime-time scripted American series since the late 1950s to air a full season live — a feat not repeated until Undateable in 2015. The live format let the writers build same-week events into scripts, including an episode staged around the 1992 presidential election. The pedigree explains the nerve: Roc's four principals were veterans of August Wilson's stage plays, most fresh from The Piano Lesson, and the series carried a theater company's discipline into a sitcom's schedule. The graph files Roc as the Fox bloc's dramatic conscience — the live-wire entry in a decade of taped ones.

name: Ray (2004 film)
description: Ray, directed by Taylor Hackford and written by James L. White, was released by Universal Pictures on October 29, 2004 — an independently produced biography of Ray Charles that follows the singer from his Florida childhood and the loss of his sight through the Atlantic Records years to the creation of a sound that fused gospel, blues, and country into soul. Jamie Foxx's performance won the Academy Award for Best Actor, and the film also won for Best Sound Mixing, from six nominations including Best Picture. Foxx won all five major lead-actor honors for the role — Oscar, Golden Globe, BAFTA, Screen Actors Guild, and Critics' Choice — only the second actor ever to sweep them. The film arrived shadowed by its subject's absence: Charles had been set to attend a screening of the completed picture but died in June 2004, four months before release, and the film is dedicated to his memory. The graph files Ray as the music-biography shelf's standard: the performance by which later singer-portrayals are measured, made while its subject could still almost see it.

name: Rev. Charles Jenkins
aliases: Charles Jenkins; Pastor Charles Jenkins; Charles Jenkins II
description: Charles Jenkins is a St. Petersburg, Florida-born pastor and gospel recording artist who, at about twenty-five, succeeded a legend: on December 8, 2000, he followed Rev. Clay Evans as senior pastor of Chicago's Fellowship Missionary Baptist Church, the congregation Evans had founded fifty years earlier. Licensed to preach at sixteen and ordained at eighteen, Jenkins joined Fellowship's staff in 1998 and led the church — styled Fellowship Chicago — for nineteen years, writing the praise anthem "Awesome," a Billboard-topping gospel song recorded with the church's choir, and releasing albums including The Best of Both Worlds (2012). He retired from Fellowship on December 31, 2019, handing the pulpit to Rev. Reginald Sharpe Jr. with Evans's blessing — a rare, orderly two-step succession in Black Baptist life.

name: Rev. Maceo Woods
aliases: Maceo Len Woods; Pastor Maceo L. Woods; Reverend Maceo Woods
description: Reverend Maceo Len Woods (April 23, 1932 – January 11, 2020) was a Chicago gospel organist, recording artist, and founding pastor whose Christian Tabernacle Choir helped define postwar Chicago gospel. Born on Chicago's South Side, he studied at Moody Bible Institute and served as music minister at Hyde Park Bible Church before founding Christian Tabernacle Church at 47th and Prairie in 1959. His recording career began in 1954 with “Amazing Grace” on Vee-Jay Records, which sold more than 200,000 copies; across 25 albums for labels including Vee-Jay, Volt/Stax, Savoy, and Arista, his only Billboard chart entry, Hello Sunshine (Volt, 1970), reached No. 45 on the R&B Albums chart, its title song No. 28 on the R&B Singles chart. He helped organize the Chicago Gospel Music Festival, hosted the late-night Midnight Gospel radio program, and in the early 1960s brought the Rev. C. L. Franklin — and his daughter Aretha — to Chicago for a gospel program. The Stellar Awards gave him a Legends Award in 2014.

name: Ray Meyer
description: Raymond Joseph Meyer (December 18, 1913 – March 17, 2006) was head coach of DePaul University men's basketball for 42 seasons (1942–1984) and the defining figure of Chicago college basketball. A Chicagoan who played and served as an assistant at Notre Dame, he built DePaul into a national program: NCAA Final Fours in 1943 and 1979, and the 1945 National Invitation Tournament championship — then treated as a national title — behind George Mikan, the awkward Archbishop Quigley Seminary student Meyer remade with coordination drills, jump rope, and dance lessons into the game's first dominant big man. Meyer retired with a 724–354 record and 37 winning seasons, then stayed on the microphone for a streak of 1,467 consecutive DePaul games coached or broadcast. He was inducted into the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame in 1979, while still coaching, and was named Associated Press Coach of the Year in 1980 and 1984. A second thread runs through his tenure: in 1954 his program fielded William C. Robinzine Sr., DePaul's first Black player. DePaul's home court carries the name Ray and Marge Meyer Court.

name: Roy Ayers Ubiquity
description: Roy Ayers Ubiquity was the band formed in 1970 by vibraphonist Roy Ayers (CTL-E-5291) after he left Herbie Mann's group, taking its name from Ayers's 1970 album Ubiquity — a word he chose because it meant being everywhere at once. Recording for Polydor, the rotating collective — whose players included Sonny Fortune, Billy Cobham, Alphonse Mouzon, Omar Hakim, Bernard Purdie, and Edwin Birdsong — moved from electric jazz toward R&B, funk, and disco across albums including He's Coming (1972), Red, Black & Green (1973), Mystic Voyage (1975), and Vibrations (1976). Its best-known record, Everybody Loves the Sunshine (1976, CTL-E-5292), carried one of the most sampled title tracks in popular music. The Ubiquity billing receded in the late 1970s as Ayers's work moved toward solo billing on Polydor and Columbia.

name: RDCWorld
aliases: RDCworld1; Real Dreams Change the World
description: RDCWorld (Real Dreams Change the World) is a Texas-based comedy and content group founded in Waco by Mark Phillips and Affiong Harris, who began making videos together in 2012. Working with friends including Leland Manigo and Desmond Johnson, the group built a mass audience on YouTube and Instagram with sketches about anime, video games, sports, and Black culture — series such as Anime House and Black Avengers turned fandom arguments into signature comedy. In 2018 the group founded Dream Con, its own anime and gaming convention, which grew from Arlington to Austin and, in 2025, to Houston's George R. Brown Convention Center, drawing 32,674 paid attendees and a reported $19.2 million in economic impact. CultureTechLens profiled RDCWorld in Short #93, published October 13, 2026.

name: Rashard Griffith
description: Rashard Griffith, born Rashard Nathan Griffith on October 8, 1974, in Chicago, Illinois, is an American former professional basketball center. He starred first at King High School in Chicago, where he was named Illinois Mr. Basketball in 1993, and then at the University of Wisconsin from 1993 to 1995. With Michael Finley, he helped lead Wisconsin to its first NCAA Tournament appearance in 47 years in 1994. The Milwaukee Bucks selected him 38th overall in the second round of the 1995 NBA draft, but he never played an NBA regular-season game and instead built a long European career. He played for Tofaş in Turkey, Maccabi Tel Aviv in Israel, and clubs in Italy, Spain, Puerto Rico, and Romania. With Kinder Bologna he won the EuroLeague championship in 2001. He retired in 2010 after playing for CSU Asesoft Ploiești. Decades later he returned to Wisconsin, graduated in May 2020 with a degree in community and nonprofit leadership, and later coached girls' basketball at Middleton High School.

name: Robert Peters
description: Robert Peters, born Robert J. Peters on April 26, 1985, in Chicago, Illinois, is an American politician serving as the Democratic state senator for Illinois's 13th district, a South Side Chicago seat once held by Barack Obama. Peters was born with a speech impediment and hearing loss and was adopted by a social worker and a civil-rights lawyer. He graduated from Mount Carmel High School and earned a bachelor's degree from Kansas State University. Before entering the Senate he worked as a community and political organizer, serving as political director of The People's Lobby and Reclaim Chicago and campaigning to end cash bail. Appointed on January 6, 2019, to succeed Kwame Raoul, who had become Illinois attorney general, he was elected in 2020 and re-elected in 2024. He chaired the Senate's Black Caucus within the Illinois Legislative Black Caucus from 2021 to 2024 and became Majority Whip of the Senate Democratic Caucus in 2025. In May 2025 he launched a campaign for Illinois's 2nd congressional district.

name: Rah Digga
aliases: Rashia Tashan Fisher; Rashia Fisher; Harriet Thugman
description: Rah Digga (born Rashia Tashan Fisher on December 18, 1974, in Newark, New Jersey) is the MC's MC of the Flipmode era — AllMusic calls her one of rap's most prominent women MCs. She studied electrical engineering at the New Jersey Institute of Technology, came up through the Outsidaz, and was first heard nationally on the Fugees' "Cowboys" from The Score (1996). Spotted by Q-Tip at the Lyricist Lounge, she was introduced to Busta Rhymes and became the first lady of his Flipmode Squad, appearing on the crew's gold album The Imperial (1998). Her solo debut Dirty Harriet (2000) reached the Billboard 200's top twenty on singles like "Tight" and "Imperial." She then crossed to film as Maggie in Thirteen Ghosts (2001) — the appearance the CTL Short bills — and released her second solo album, Classic, in 2010. name: Robin Harris
description: Robin Harris, born Robin Hughes Harris on August 30, 1953, in Chicago, Illinois, was an American comedian and actor best known for his “Bébé's Kids” routine. The son of Earl Harris, a welder, and Mattie Harris, a factory seamstress, he was born at the family home at 4640 South Drexel Avenue; the family moved to Los Angeles in 1961, where he attended Manual Arts High School, and he went on to Ottawa University in Kansas. Harris debuted at The Comedy Store in 1980 and worked as master of ceremonies at the Comedy Act Theater in the mid-1980s. His film roles came in a rush: a bartender in I'm Gonna Git You Sucka (1988), Sweet Dick Willie in Spike Lee's Do the Right Thing (1989), Harlem Nights (1989), and Pop in House Party (1990), a performance that earned a posthumous Independent Spirit Award nomination. On March 18, 1990, hours after a sold-out performance in his hometown, Harris died of heart failure at Chicago's Four Seasons Hotel, aged 36. The Hudlin brothers' animated Bébé's Kids (1992) carried his signature routine to the screen after his death.

name: Rod Wave
description: Rod Wave, born Rodarius Marcell Green on 27 August in St. Petersburg, Florida, is an American rapper and singer whose trap-soul blend pairs rap cadence with R&B confession. Signed to Alamo Records through Hit House Entertainment, he broke through with "Heart on Ice" (2019), which went viral on TikTok and reached No. 25 on the Hot 100. His albums run Ghetto Gospel (2019), Pray 4 Love (2020), SoulFly (2021), Beautiful Mind (2022), Nostalgia (2023) and Last Lap (2024). Nostalgia debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 with 137,000 first-week units — his third consecutive No. 1 — and Last Lap debuted at No. 2 on the Billboard 200 and No. 1 on Top R&B/Hip-Hop Albums with 127,000 units. His birth year is contested between 1998 and 1999 across sources and is carried here unresolved.

name: RCA Records
aliases: RCA Victor; Victor Talking Machine Company; RCA Victor Records
description: RCA Records is an American record label whose lineage begins with the Victor Talking Machine Company, incorporated in Camden, New Jersey, in 1901 by Eldridge R. Johnson with the patents of gramophone inventor Emile Berliner. Victor became one of the world's leading record companies before the Radio Corporation of America acquired it in 1929, after which it operated as RCA Victor. Black artists are present from the label's first years: Broadway performers Bert Williams and George Walker recorded for Victor in 1901, and in 1914 Victor recorded Black composer James Reese Europe directing the Castle House Orchestra, though Europe's name was left off the record's advertising. RCA Victor's East 24th Street studio in New York, operating from 1928 to 1969, hosted recordings by the Isley Brothers, Harry Belafonte, Lena Horne, Della Reese and Charles Mingus, among others. In 1960 Sam Cooke signed with RCA, where he recorded a run of hits; under his agreement he retained control of the copyrights to his music, and his posthumously released 'A Change Is Gonna Come' was later selected by the Library of Congress for preservation.

name: Ruff Ryders
aliases: Ruff Ryders Entertainment; Ryde or Die
description: Ruff Ryders is the Yonkers, New York hip-hop name that is two things at once: Ruff Ryders Entertainment, the record label and management company founded in 1988 by siblings Joaquin 'Waah' Dean, Darin 'Dee' Dean and Chivon Dean, and the loose-knit collective of the label's core signees that the same name denotes. The Deans first built their reputation managing DMX and The Lox; after DMX's breakthrough, the company opened its own label imprint through Interscope Records. The collective announced itself with the compilation Ryde or Die Vol. 1 (April 27, 1999), which debuted at number one on the Billboard 200, was certified platinum by the RIAA on June 2, 1999, and carried Eve's first appearance as a Ruff Ryder — the 'First Lady' role she built her career on. The Deans' nephew Swizz Beatz was the roster's principal producer. Three further Ryde or Die volumes followed through 2005. In 2010 the founders revamped the brand as the distribution venture Ruff Ryders Indy; one account of that move calls it the end of Ruff Ryders Entertainment, while the label's reference entry still lists its status as active — the conflict is carried openly in this packet.

name: Run the Jewels
description: Run the Jewels is the hip-hop duo of Brooklyn rapper-producer El-P and Atlanta rapper Killer Mike. The partnership grew directly out of El-P's production of Killer Mike's solo album R.A.P. Music (2012); the two formed Run the Jewels in 2013 and released their self-titled debut that June on Fool's Gold Records as a free download. Run the Jewels 2 (2014) moved the duo from underground acclaim to the Billboard 200, and its crowd-funded cat-sound remix, Meow the Jewels (2015), sent its proceeds to charity. Run the Jewels 3, released digitally on December 24, 2016, became the duo's first number one on Billboard's rap and R&B/hip-hop album charts, and RTJ4 (2020) reached the Top Ten of the Billboard 200 in both the United States and the United Kingdom. The duo's work with Danger Mouse and Big Boi on 'Chase Me' (2017) earned a Grammy nomination for Best Rap Song. AllMusic characterizes the pair's records as hard-hitting and ominous in production, trading aggressive and wry rhymes on social issues, life and death; the graph already holds Killer Mike's record (CTL-E-5677), and this record is the duo endpoint it was missing.

name: Ronaldinho
aliases: Ronaldo de Assis Moreira; Ronaldinho Gaúcho; O Bruxo
description: Ronaldinho, born Ronaldo de Assis Moreira on 21 March 1980 in Porto Alegre, Brazil, is a Brazilian attacking midfielder and winger renowned for his dribbling, tricks and free-kick accuracy. He debuted for Grêmio in 1998, moved to Paris Saint-Germain in 2001 and reached his prime at FC Barcelona from 2003, where he won the FIFA World Player of the Year award in 2004 and 2005, the 2005 Ballon d'Or, two La Liga titles and the 2006 UEFA Champions League; he is widely credited with elevating Barcelona in the early 2000s. With Brazil he won the 1999 Copa América and the 2002 World Cup. He later played for AC Milan, Flamengo and Atlético Mineiro, winning the 2013 Copa Libertadores, and his last professional club was Fluminense in 2015. In August 2026 he was presented by Italian Serie C club Ravenna, where he also took a stake; Reuters reported he stopped short of confirming whether he would play again.

name: Raphinha
description: Raphinha, born Raphael Dias Belloli on 14 December 1996 in Porto Alegre, Brazil, is a Brazilian winger for FC Barcelona and the Brazil national team. Raised in Restinga, a peripheral neighbourhood of Porto Alegre, he was rejected in trials at Internacional and Grêmio and played neighbourhood várzea football before joining Avaí and moving to Portugal's Vitória Guimarães in 2016. Spells at Sporting CP, where he won the 2019 Taça de Portugal and Taça da Liga, and Rennes followed, before two Premier League seasons at Leeds United, where Barcelona's official biography credits him with 17 goals. He joined Barcelona in July 2022 and helped the club to the La Liga title in his first season. His 2024–25 campaign was career-defining: 34 goals in all competitions as Barcelona won a domestic treble of La Liga, the Copa del Rey and the Spanish Super Cup, and he finished fifth in the 2025 Ballon d'Or voting.

name: Roberto Carlos
aliases: Roberto Carlos da Silva Rocha; RC3
description: Roberto Carlos, born Roberto Carlos da Silva Rocha on 10 April 1973 in Garça, São Paulo, Brazil, is a Brazilian former footballer described as the most offensive-minded left-back in the history of the game. He began his career in Brazil as a forward before converting to left-back, and after Palmeiras and one season at Inter Milan he joined Real Madrid in 1996, spending 11 seasons there with 584 appearances and 71 goals in all competitions, winning four La Liga titles and three UEFA Champions Leagues. For Brazil he earned 125 caps, reached the 1998 World Cup final and won the 2002 World Cup in Korea and Japan; he was runner-up for the FIFA World Player of the Year in 1997 and for the Ballon d'Or in 2002. He is remembered above all for a bending 40-yard free kick against France at the 1997 Tournoi de France. His later career took in Fenerbahçe, Corinthians, Anzhi Makhachkala and Delhi Dynamos, where he also served as player-manager.

name: Rosenwald Schools
aliases: Rosenwald School Program; Rosenwald school-building program
description: The Rosenwald Schools were the product of a partnership between Booker T. Washington of Tuskegee Institute and Julius Rosenwald, president of Sears, Roebuck and Company in Chicago. With Washington's encouragement, Rosenwald funded Tuskegee to build six schools for African-American children in rural Alabama in 1913, then expanded the effort; in 1917 he established the Julius Rosenwald Fund, and from 1917 to 1932 the Fund ran the rural school-building program across the segregated South. The model required matching commitment: Black communities raised funds and donated property and labor, and white school boards had to agree to operate and maintain the schools, which were built to designs developed at Tuskegee. Counts vary by what is counted, and this record does not blend them: the Library of Congress guide, quoting the Fund-era record, gives 4,977 schools completed by 1932 serving 663,615 students in 15 states, while the National Park Service history gives 5,357 buildings of all types by 1932 and 4,978 schools once a final 1936 school is included. About one-third of Black children in the South were educated in these schools in their active years.

name: Romeo Santos
aliases: Anthony Santos; Anthony "Romeo" Santos; The King of Bachata
description: Romeo Santos, born Anthony Santos on 21 July 1981 in the Bronx, New York City, is a Dominican-American singer, songwriter and producer known as the King of Bachata. Born to a Dominican father and a Puerto Rican mother, he sang in a church choir as a child and co-founded the bachata group Aventura in the Bronx, serving as its lead vocalist, frontman and principal songwriter. Aventura fused bachata with R&B, hip-hop and pop, breaking through internationally with “Obsesión,” which spent sixteen weeks at No. 1 in Italy. After Aventura split in 2011, Santos launched a solo career with Fórmula, Vol. 1 (2011), followed by Fórmula, Vol. 2 (2014), carrying “Propuesta Indecente” and “Odio,” featuring Drake, and sold-out stadium shows including Yankee Stadium. Golden (2017), Utopía (2019) and Fórmula, Vol. 3 (2022) completed his solo run through the trilogy. In November 2025 he released Better Late Than Never, a collaborative album with Prince Royce that debuted at No. 1 on Billboard's Top Tropical Albums, and in 2026 he co-headlined the Mejor Tarde Que Nunca tour across the United States, Europe and Latin America.

name: Russell Westbrook
description: Russell Westbrook, born 12 November 1988 in Long Beach, California, and raised in the Los Angeles area, is an American former point guard who retired in August 2026 as the NBA's all-time leader in triple-doubles. After Leuzinger High School in Lawndale and two seasons at UCLA, reaching consecutive Final Fours, he was drafted fourth overall in 2008 by Seattle, just before the franchise became the Oklahoma City Thunder. In eleven seasons in Oklahoma City he won the 2016-17 Most Valuable Player award, averaging a triple-double that season — a feat he repeated three more times — and set the single-season record with 42 triple-doubles. A nine-time All-Star, two-time scoring champion and three-time assists leader, he later played for Houston, Washington, the Los Angeles Lakers, the Los Angeles Clippers and Denver before closing with Sacramento in 2025-26, averaging 15.2 points, 6.7 assists and 5.4 rebounds in 64 games. He won Olympic gold at London 2012, was named to the NBA 75th Anniversary Team, and founded the Why Not? Foundation in 2012 for underserved communities in Los Angeles and beyond. He finished with 209 career triple-doubles.

name: Roberto Clemente
aliases: Roberto Enrique Clemente Walker; The Great One
description: Roberto Enrique Clemente Walker, born 18 August 1934 in Carolina, Puerto Rico, was a proud Afro-Latino right fielder who played all 18 of his major league seasons (1955–1972) for the Pittsburgh Pirates. The youngest child of a sugarcane worker and a laundress, he confronted Jim Crow segregation directly when the Pirates traveled in the South, and he defended Black and Latino players throughout his career. On the field he collected exactly 3,000 hits, batted .317, won four National League batting titles, twelve consecutive Gold Gloves and the 1966 NL MVP Award, and starred for World Series champions in 1960 and 1971, when he was World Series MVP. On 31 December 1972 he died in a plane crash off Isla Verde while personally accompanying earthquake-relief supplies to Nicaragua. In 1973 he became the first Latin American player inducted into the Baseball Hall of Fame.

name: Ronald Acuña Jr.
aliases: Ronald José Acuña Blanco; El Abusador
description: Ronald Acuña Jr., born 18 December 1997 in La Guaira, Venezuela, is the Atlanta Braves' right fielder and one of the most electrifying players of his generation. He debuted on 25 April 2018, won the National League Rookie of the Year Award, and in 2023 produced a historic MVP season as the founding member of the 40-home-run, 70-stolen-base club. Injuries — including two major knee injuries — have repeatedly interrupted him, and he was named the NL Comeback Player of the Year in 2025 after returning from an ACL tear. In September 2026 he hit his 200th career home run, becoming the fastest player ever to pair 200 home runs with 200 stolen bases (he reached the milestone with 225 steals). name: Roy Campanella
description: Roy Campanella (born November 19, 1921, Philadelphia; died June 26, 1993, Woodland Hills, California) was a catcher who starred on both sides of baseball's color line. He began in the Negro leagues as a teenager with the Washington Elite Giants in 1937 and became a star with the Baltimore Elite Giants, also playing in the Mexican League, before joining the Brooklyn Dodgers organization. He debuted in the majors on April 20, 1948, and caught for Brooklyn for ten seasons, winning the National League Most Valuable Player award three times, in 1951, 1953, and 1955, and catching the Dodgers' 1955 World Series championship team. In 1953 he set single-season records for a catcher with 41 home runs and 142 runs batted in. An automobile accident in January 1958 left him paralyzed and ended his playing career; he remained with the Dodgers in scouting and community roles and entered the Baseball Hall of Fame in 1969.

name: Rebeca Andrade
description: Rebeca Rodrigues de Andrade, born 8 May 1999 in Guarulhos, São Paulo, is a Brazilian artistic gymnast and the most decorated Brazilian Olympian in any discipline. Raised by her mother Rosa, a house cleaner, in a family of eight children, she walked nearly two hours to training on days the family could not afford the bus. Three anterior cruciate ligament surgeries between 2015 and 2019 nearly ended her career. At the Tokyo Olympics she won gold on vault and silver in the all-around, becoming the first Brazilian female gymnast to win an Olympic medal. She was world all-around champion in 2022 and world vault champion in 2021 and 2023, and she won the 2025 Laureus Comeback of the Year award. At Paris 2024 she won floor gold ahead of Simone Biles, all-around and vault silver, and team bronze — Brazil's first Olympic team medal — closing the Games on the first all-Black podium in Olympic gymnastics history. Her six Olympic medals are a Brazilian record. After a gap year in 2025 she returned in 2026, winning Pan American vault gold and leading Brazil at the World Championships in Rotterdam, having retired from floor exercise for good.

name: Red Saunders
description: Red Saunders, born Theodore Dudley Saunders on March 2, 1912 in Memphis, Tennessee, was an American jazz drummer and bandleader who also played vibraphone and timpani. After his mother's death he moved to Chicago with his sister, became a professional musician in 1928, and returned to Chicago in 1934 to join Tiny Parham's band at the Savoy Ballroom. In 1937 he joined the house band at the Club DeLisa, initially led by pianist Albert Ammons, and soon took over as bandleader himself. He remained in control of the Club DeLisa house band, playing four to six shows nightly, until the club closed in 1958, apart from a hiatus from 1945 to 1947. His sidemen included singer Joe Williams, and his arrangers included Johnny Pate and Sun Ra. He recorded as a bandleader from 1945, scored an R&B chart success in 1952 with Hambone on the OKeh label, played with Duke Ellington, Louis Armstrong and Woody Herman, and led a band at Chicago's Regal Theater into the 1960s. He died in Chicago on March 5, 1981, aged 69.

name: Rickwood Field
description: Rickwood Field is a baseball park at 1137 2nd Avenue West in Birmingham, Alabama, built for the Birmingham Barons in 1910 by industrialist and team owner Rick Woodward and opened August 18, 1910. The National Park Service National Register nomination, prepared in 1992, calls it the oldest surviving baseball park in the country and records that Woodward spent $75,000 on a park modeled after Pittsburgh's Forbes Field. The nomination stresses its ethnic-heritage significance as the playing field of the Birmingham Black Barons of the Negro leagues, a source of pride to Black Birmingham, and names Satchel Paige and Willie Mays among the Black Barons greats produced there. The Barons moved their home games to Hoover after the 1988 season, and the park has since been preserved as a working museum, with the Barons playing one regular-season game a year there. In 2024 it hosted a Major League regular-season game between the St. Louis Cardinals and San Francisco Giants, a tribute to the Negro Leagues, after renovations. Mays, who began his professional career with the Black Barons in 1948, died two days before that game, a fact announced to the crowd at Rickwood that week.

name: Robert T. Motts
description: Robert T. Motts was a Chicago saloon owner, gambling figure and Republican Party organizer who founded the Pekin Theatre, the Black-owned musical and vaudeville house at 27th and State Street on Chicago's Near South Side. Born June 24, 1861, in Iowa, he left home at eighteen for St. Louis and then Chicago, worked odd jobs and as a coachman, and after the 1893 World's Fair invested in the saloon at 2700 State Street, eventually buying out his partners. Answering a 1901 call by Black businessmen for a Chicago theater controlled by Black people, and inspired, in one account, by a 1901 visit to a Paris music hall, he converted his Pekin saloon and restaurant into the Pekin Theatre, the 'Temple of Music.' It opened its first all-Black show on June 18, 1905, to an estimated crowd of 400. After a 1906 fire he rebuilt it as the New Pekin, raising capacity from 400 to 1,200, with an all-Black stock company and staff presenting original musical comedies. Thomas Bauman's University of Illinois Press study calls the Pekin Chicago's first Black-owned theater in its title. Motts died July 11, 1911, in Chicago, aged fifty.

name: RuPaul
description: RuPaul, born RuPaul Andre Charles on 17 November 1960 in San Diego, California, is an American drag queen, television host, producer, singer and actor. Raised in San Diego, he studied performing arts in Atlanta before moving to New York City, where he became a fixture of the LGBTQ nightclub scene. He achieved international fame with the 1993 single “Supermodel (You Better Work)” and in 1994 became a spokesperson for MAC Cosmetics, the first drag queen to front a major cosmetics campaign. After hosting The RuPaul Show on VH1 in the late 1990s, he created RuPaul's Drag Race, which premiered in 2009 with him as producer, host and judge. The franchise has produced eighteen United States seasons and international versions including RuPaul's Drag Race UK and Canada's Drag Race. His memoir The House of Hidden Meanings was published in March 2024, and from January to April 2026 he hosted the eighteenth season of Drag Race on MTV.

name: Ralph Abernathy
aliases: Ralph David Abernathy; Ralph David Abernathy Sr.; Rev. Ralph Abernathy
description: Ralph David Abernathy was a Baptist pastor and civil rights leader who was Martin Luther King Jr.'s chief aide and closest associate during the movement of the 1950s and 1960s. Born March 11, 1926, in Linden, Alabama, he was ordained in 1948, earned a bachelor's degree from Alabama State in 1950 and a master's from Atlanta University in 1951, and that year became pastor of First Baptist Church in Montgomery. In 1955–56 he and King organized the Montgomery bus boycott, and both men helped found the Montgomery Improvement Association. In 1957 they co-founded the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, with King as president and Abernathy as secretary-treasurer. Abernathy moved his pastorate to Atlanta in 1961 and took part in campaigns including the Albany Movement. After King's assassination in 1968 he succeeded him as SCLC president, led the Poor People's Campaign in Washington, D.C., that summer, and headed the SCLC until 1977. His autobiography appeared in 1989. He died April 17, 1990, in Atlanta, Georgia.

name: Rocky Jones
description: Rocky Jones is an American DJ, producer, and record label founder in Chicago house music. Discogs lists his real name as Alexander M. Alcarese and identifies him as the founder, with Benji Espinoza, of D.J. International Records and its successor DJ International Multimedia. Resident Advisor reports that Jones founded D.J. International in Chicago in the mid-1980s, based across the street from the Warehouse club; DJ Mag dates the founding, with Espinoza, to 1985. The label's first releases included J.M. Silk's 'Music Is the Key,' and its 1986 compilation The House Sound of Chicago carried Steve 'Silk' Hurley's 'Jack Your Body,' Farley 'Jackmaster' Funk's 'Love Can't Turn Around,' and Marshall Jefferson's 'Move Your Body.' The label also released Joe Smooth's 'Promised Land' and, in 2017, began a remastered digital reissue campaign of 130 singles from a catalogue by then controlled by Universal Music. In 2021 the label relaunched under exclusive license to Last Man Music with Jones, its original founder, still at its helm.

name: Rahim Thompson
description: Rahim Thompson is Senior Program Manager at the Illinois Holocaust Museum & Education Center in Skokie, Illinois, where he has developed more than 200 public programs spanning antisemitism, genocide, LGBTQ+ rights and racial justice. The Association of Midwest Museums named him a 2025 Promising Leadership Award honoree; PMI lists him among its Future 50 honorees, and IPMA named him its Young Project Manager of the Year 2025 (Gold). His background spans project management, journalism and production. He was named to WVON's 40 Under 40 Game Changers Class of 2026.

name: Ronnie Mosley
description: Ronnie Mosley is the Alderman of Chicago's 21st Ward on the Far South Side — a ward spanning parts of Washington Heights, West Pullman, Morgan Park, Auburn Gresham, Beverly, Chatham and Roseland — sworn in on May 15, 2023 after winning the 2023 runoff election with 52% and succeeding Howard Brookins; at his election he was the City Council's youngest member. Before office he co-founded the policy and organizing firm Homegrown Strategy Group (2017) and worked in Alderman Michelle A. Harris's office (2015–2017). He was named to WVON's 40 Under 40 Game Changers Class of 2026.
